Reprieve

/rih-PREEV/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Reprieve means an official postponement of a punishment or unwanted event — the trouble is delayed for a time, not canceled

Reprieve means an official postponement of a punishment or unwanted event — the trouble is delayed for a time, not canceled. The vendor won a reprieve when the hospital agreed to push back the contract's termination date while new terms were negotiated.

Worked Example

The century-old theater received a reprieve from demolition while the preservationists' paperwork made its way through the county office.

The wrecking crews have not been called off forever — the demolition is only postponed while the review happens. A delay with the threat still hanging in the air is exactly what a reprieve is.

How Reprieve Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

stay

stay: an official halt or delay of a legal action

postponement

postponement: the moving of something to a later time

deferral

deferral: an official decision to put something off

Antonyms

enforcement

enforcement: carrying a punishment out right away

resumption

resumption: starting something up again after a pause

How Strong Is It? — delay → reprieve → pardon

delay vs. reprieve

delay vs. reprieve: A delay is any small postponement at all — your bus can be delayed without anyone facing punishment, so it is much weaker and more everyday than a reprieve.

pardon vs. reprieve

pardon vs. reprieve: A pardon goes much further than a reprieve: it wipes the punishment away forever, while a reprieve only holds it off for a time.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back, again (Latin)

Root — -prieve

Root — -prieve: to take, seize — from Latin prehendere, arriving through Old French repris, 'taken back'

Put it together

Put it together: Re- ('back') plus a French descendant of Latin prehendere ('to take, seize'): a reprieve literally 'takes back' a prisoner from punishment for a while. The sentence waits — it does not disappear.

Use the root in a new word: comprehend

Use the root in a new word: comprehend: It took Jonah a moment to comprehend the map — the same 'seize' root that lets a reprieve take a prisoner back lets your mind take hold of an idea.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal, with common figurative use

A reprieve is strictly temporary — it postpones a punishment or dreaded event but never erases it, so don't use it where you mean a pardon or a cancellation. It also thrives figuratively in everyday writing: a cool morning can be 'a brief reprieve from the heat wave.' Don't confuse it with reprise, a repeated section of music.
